title: NON-PENETRATING & MICRO-INVASIVE GLAUCOMA SURGERY
summary: An exhaustive guide to advanced surgical drainage techniques that avoid initial AC penetration and the evolving landscape of MIGS devices. This poster covers mechanisms, procedural outlines, variations, and complications for non-penetrating and micro-invasive procedures.

sections.title: Non-penetrating Glaucoma Surgery (NPGS) Overview
sections.content: Non-penetrating glaucoma surgery (NPGS) describes a group of techniques in which improved aqueous drainage is achieved surgically without penetrating into the AC at the time of initial surgery. Controversy continues regarding their long-term success rate, partly due to the long learning curve associated with these challenging techniques. It is likely that, in experienced hands, NPGS with augmentation can achieve similar long-term success to that seen with penetrating glaucoma surgery, but final IOPs are often higher than after augmented trabeculectomy surgery.

sections.title: Early Risks vs. Serious Complications
content: Although NPGS has a lower rate of early hypotony after surgery, serious complications have been described:
Severe hypotony
Endophthalmitis
Suprachoroidal haemorrhage

branches: Mechanism: Guarded filtration (like trabeculectomy); drainage rate controlled at TM/Descemet's membrane instead of scleral flap.
Outline: Formation of conjunctival and superficial scleral flaps.
Deep (90% depth) scleral flap to expose Schlemm's canal.
Schlemm's canal deroofed; endothelium and juxtacanalicular TM peeled off to improve drainage.
Deep scleral flap part excised to form deep sclerectomy space.
Final: Antifibrotics may be applied, implant may be inserted; conjunctival flap closed.

sections.title: Deep Sclerectomy Variations
content: Antifibrotics: Used in high-risk cases to reduce intrascleral scarring. No benefit demonstrated with 5-FU; small studies show improved IOP control with MMC.14
Implants: Inserted into deep scleral space to maintain space during healing and form 'intrascleral bleb'.
Absorbable Implants: e.g. Aquaflow or SKGel.
Non-absorbable Implants: e.g. t Flux.

Goniopuncture: Nd-yAG goniopuncture used as 2° procedure if IOP control is insufficient; effectively converts it to a penetrating procedure. performed in about half of cases in one study. Sight-threatening complications (hypotony) reported.

rows: Expected (with deep AC); may transiently affect vision.
Inadequate dissection of TM/Descemet's membrane (treated with Nd-yAG goniopuncture).
Rupture of TM/Descemet's membrane by mild trauma (rubbing, Valsalva), causing iris prolapse and drainage blockage (requires revision/conversion to trabeculectomy).
PAS formation blocking drainage site (reversible with laser iridoplasty).
Detachment of Descemet's membrane (very rare). All complications of penetrating surgery have been reported.

sections.title: Viscocanalostomy Details
content: Mechanism: Proposed to increase aqueous flow into Schlemm's canal (little evidence to support).
Procedure: Creation of conjunctival, superficial, and deep scleral flaps; deroofing of Schlemm's canal.
Key Feature: Schlemm's canal is opened with a viscoelastic to improve drainage.
Closure: Superficial scleral flap tightly sutured to minimize sub-Tenon's filtration, encouraging canal drainage.
Variations: Both antifibrotics and implants may be used.
Complications: Similar to deep sclerectomy. Detachment of Descemet's membrane (at time of viscoelastic injection) is more common but still uncommon.

sections.title: Micro-invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS) Landscape
sections.content: Over the past decade, there has been a proliferation in the number of MIGS devices developed, in an attempt to improve the safety and ease of glaucoma surgery. these devices target Schlemm’s canal, the suprachoroidal space, and the sub-tenon’s space. MIGS devices can be used alone or in combination with phaco cataract surgery. however, IOP reduction achieved with the use of these devices are less than IOP reduction achieved with trabeculectomy. therefore, at present, their role is in the management of early to moderate glaucoma, and their role in advanced disease has not been defined.

sections.title: Schlemm's Canal Procedures (Part 1)
content: iStent: Small transtrabecular titanium stent (1mm x 0.3mm). Drains aqueous from AC into Schlemm's canal. Placed through 2.8mm clear corneal incision with gonioscopy lens. Inserted in inferonasal quadrant via introducer. Positive sign: Immediate blood reflux from Schlemm's canal through/around snorkel. For phaco, pseudophakic, or phakic eyes. Advanced glaucoma role under evaluation.
Hydrus stent: 8mm nitinol (nickel-titanium alloy) stent. Functions as intracanalicular scaffold in Schlemm's canal and dilates the canal. Early data are promising.
Trabectome: Thermal cautery device ablating 2- to 4-clock-hour segment of TM and Schlemm's canal under direct gonioscopy. Connects AC directly with collector channels. Phaco/phakic/pseudophakic use.

sections.title: Schlemm's Canal Procedures (Part 2)
content: Kahook dual blade: Microblade designed to strip a section of TM and anterior wall of Schlemm's canal (similar principle to Trabectome).
Ab interno canaloplasty (ABiC): Microcatheter threaded 360° around Schlemm's canal under gonioscopic view; viscoelastic used to mechanically dilate canal.
Ab externo canaloplasty: Uses 9-0 or 10-0 prolene suture through 360° of Schlemm's canal with microcatheter and viscoelastic. Involves construction of a deep sclerectomy-type flap for access.

sections.title: Suprachoroidal Procedures
content: CyPass Micro-Stent: Supraciliary microstent implanted through 1.5mm clear corneal incision. Increases uveoscleral outflow (AC to suprachoroidal space). Inserted over micro-guidewire creating small cyclodialysis cleft.
Solx Gold Shunt: Small shunt placed into supraciliary space through 3mm incision to increase uveoscleral outflow. Direct access from AC to suprachoroidal space.
Failure Risk: All current supraciliary microstents may develop fibrosis around the device.

sections.title: Sub-Tenon's Microshunt Procedures
content: Xen and Innfocus: Connect AC to sub-Tenon's space for traditional filtering bleb. Xen uses a gelatin implant.
Adjuvant MMC: Anti-scarring MMC may be injected subconjunctivally at surgery.
PI: Peripheral iridectomy is NOT performed in these procedures.
Maintenance: Bleb needling revision may be required if fibrosis occurs.
Ex-Press: Small stainless steel minishunt. Drains AC to sub-Tenon's space. Used with standard trabeculectomy. PI is NOT performed.
